source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: A Many Labs replication project
finding: Numeric anchoring from Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) replicated in every one of 36 samples, with effects far larger than the original. Gain/loss framing replicated at about half the original size.
numbers: N over 6,000, 36 samples. Anchoring median d: babies born 2.43, Mt Everest 2.00, Chicago 1.88, distance to NYC 1.18. Original (pooled over 15 items) d = 0.93. Proportion of samples significant in expected direction = 1.00 for all four items. Gain vs loss framing: original d 1.13, replication about 0.60. 11 of 13 effects replicated; flag priming and currency priming did not.
quote: The original studies produced underestimates of some effects (e.g., anchoring-and-adjustment and allowed versus forbidden message framing)
limits: Participants saw the anchor and then gave an estimate only (no higher/lower question first). Original was within-subject test-retest, replication between-subjects, so d values are not strictly comparable. Anchoring items had the largest heterogeneity across samples; authors suggest differences in knowledge of the quantity. Moderation by country or lab/online was small (partial eta squared at most .022).
agent_relevance: A planted number moves estimates by 1 to 2.4 standard deviations in a robust, cross-sample way. Treat any number in the prompt, including a stated guess, as a strong pull on the first answer. S1 should strip or mark such numbers before the model estimates.

source: Hertwig and Gigerenzer (1999) The 'conjunction fallacy' revisited: How intelligent inferences look like reasoning errors
finding: Many Linda-problem conjunction errors come from reading 'probability' as something non-mathematical (plausibility, typicality). When wording removes that reading, violations fall sharply.
numbers: Study 1: 83% (15 of 18) violated the conjunction rule in the standard probability ranking. Study 2 standard condition: 88% (21 of 24) and 82% (18 of 22). With a frequency format, Study 3: 0% (0 of 20); Study 4: 13% (3 of 23). Median violation in the probability ranking format across reviewed studies = 87%; in the frequency estimation format = 17%.
limits: Small cell sizes (about 20 per cell). Frequency format also adds extensional cues, so format and wording effects are partly confounded; the authors say about half of a 70-point difference is due to response mode. Kahneman and Tversky disputed this reading.
agent_relevance: Wording of the question can flip a 'bias' on or off. The agent should ask for counts or frequencies ('out of 100 women like Linda, how many...') in S1, not bare probabilities.

source: Hertwig and Gigerenzer (1999), section on rival wording and clarification manipulations (review of earlier studies)
finding: Across earlier studies, adding a clarifying phrase or a betting instruction cuts conjunction errors by 20 to 60 points, but never to zero in the probability format. Frequency format effect varies a lot by study.
numbers: Frequency vs probability violations: Tversky and Kahneman 58% vs 25%; Fiedler 73% vs 23%; Reeves and Lockhart 59% vs 35%; Jones et al. 85% vs 81% (no effect). Clarifying phrase: 89% to 57%, and 77% to 56% (Messer and Griggs). Politzer and Noveck rephrasing: 77% to 29%. Betting instruction: 89% to 56% (33 points).
limits: Reviewed by the paper's authors, who argue for the pragmatic account; numbers are as they report them from the primary studies. Results come from different problems and populations.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that the frequency format does not always help (Jones et al. shows 81%). Do not assume a rewrite fixes the error; the wording needs a test on our own model.

source: Hertwig and Gigerenzer (1999), within-subject versus between-subject design discussion
finding: Whether a bias shows depends on design. In between-subject designs the conjunction and base-rate errors look larger. In within-subject designs people often use base rates and the 'fallacy' shrinks.
numbers: Class inclusion: 26% (8 of 31) violated in a between-subjects variant. Dulany and Hilton: by their criterion only 26% of participants read the item in the formal sense. Cited from Varey, Mellers and Birnbaum (1990): in within-subject comparisons the evidence for a base-rate fallacy 'disappears'.
limits: Secondhand for Varey et al.; the paper's own studies are small. Argument is partly interpretive.
agent_relevance: When the agent sees both the base rate and the case together (a within-problem comparison), it is likelier to use both. S1 should place the base rate next to the case description in the same slot.

source: Lewinski (2015) Commentary: Extensional versus intuitive reasoning (on Tversky and Kahneman 1983)
finding: Short commentary that restates that over 80% fail the conjunction rule in Linda, and that the pragmatic reading (Hertwig and Gigerenzer 1999) and bounded rationality offer rival accounts.
numbers: Over 80% of participants in the Linda problem; the original paper cited about 1,100 times in Web of Science as of Nov 2015.
limits: Commentary, no new data. Low weight.
agent_relevance: Shows the field still treats Linda as contested: effect real, interpretation disputed.

source: Toplak, West and Stanovich (2011) The Cognitive Reflection Test as a predictor of performance on heuristics-and-biases tasks
finding: Heuristics-and-biases tasks vary hugely in how many people get them right. The three-item CRT predicts overall rational-thinking score better than cognitive ability, thinking dispositions or executive function, and keeps adding variance after they are controlled.
numbers: N = 346 students. Percent correct: causal base rate 53.8; hospital sample-size 28.6; squash sample-size 15.6; regression to mean 40.2; gambler's fallacy 69.4 and 92.2; conjunction 19.1; covariation 36.1; Bayesian reasoning 22.3; framing 62.7; sunk cost 64.2; outcome bias 72.0. CRT mean 0.7 of 3; 55.8% solved none. CRT correlated r = .49 with the rational-thinking composite; cognitive ability r = .41.
limits: University students, one sample. Correlational. CRT is partly numerical ability.
agent_relevance: Errors cluster in 'miserly' processing, not only in ability. A scaffold that forces a second look only where a quick answer conflicts with a check mirrors what CRT-style reflection does. Supports G1 (doubt on a signal) rather than blanket doubt.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: Improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: One training session (a serious computer game with personalized feedback, or an instructional video) reduced anchoring, representativeness and projection bias immediately and at a delayed follow-up, and transferred to untrained problem facets.
numbers: Experiment 2: 238 completed lab session (game 156, video 82), 192 follow-up. Overall bias d pre-post: game 1.74, video 1.75; follow-up game 1.16, video 1.07. Anchoring d: game .70 immediate, .63 follow-up; video .80, .66. Representativeness d: game 1.51 / 1.05; video 1.80 / 1.09. Projection: game 1.11 / .54; video .49 / .14. Abstract: bias reduced by at least 31.94% (games) and 18.60% (videos), persisting at least 23.57% and 19.20% later.
limits: Own measures built by the authors; anchoring subscale reliability only about .52 to .62. Convenience sample, paid. Training taught rules (conjunction, sample size, consider alternatives, reconsider first answer). Follow-up at 8 to 12 weeks, not years.
agent_relevance: Debiasing works best when it teaches the specific rule plus feedback on one's own error. For the agent this maps to code-checked rules and an error report from checks, not to a general 'be careful' line.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys and Goodman (2018) The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources
finding: A resource-rational anchoring-and-adjustment model (sampling-based adjustment with a cost-benefit stopping rule) accounts for ten known anchoring phenomena, including effects of time pressure, load, incentives and anchor extremity. The paper also reviews the moderators.
numbers: Model fit to cognitive-load data: simulated adjustments fell 18.61% under load (83.45% vs 102.06% relative adjustment), close to the empirical effect. Fitted about 14 adjustments under load vs 60 without.
limits: Model paper; moderator facts are secondhand from the cited studies (Epley and Gilovich 2006; Simmons et al. 2010; Wilson et al. 1996; Chapman and Johnson 1994). Competes with selective-accessibility accounts (Mussweiler and Strack).
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism that predicts when more thinking helps: only when adjustment direction is known and effort is cheap. Suggests more compute helps with self-generated anchors, much less with anchors planted in the prompt.

source: Lieder et al. (2018), literature review section on moderators of anchoring
finding: Moderators of human anchoring: more uncertainty about the quantity gives more anchoring; knowledgeable people are immune in one study; expertise reduces but does not abolish it; effect grows with anchor distance then flattens for absurd anchors; incentives help with self-generated anchors but usually not with provided anchors.
numbers: No pooled number. Cited: Wilson et al. 1996 (knowledgeable people immune); Northcraft and Neale 1987 (experts still anchored); Chapman and Johnson 1994 (extreme anchors add less); Simmons, LeBoeuf and Nelson 2010 (accuracy motivation helps if and only if people know the direction to adjust).
quote: accuracy motivation decreases the anchoring bias only in some cases, but not in others
limits: Secondhand summary of other papers; each cited study should be checked before relying on a single figure.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to 'be accurate' will not remove a planted anchor. Knowledge of the direction (a check or a bracket from code) is the lever.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) showed the Linda conjunction error and equal-probability answer on the hospital sample-size problem like people, but did NOT neglect the base rate in the cab problem. It gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three CRT items. Small edits to vignettes broke its answers.
numbers: Linda: chose the conjunction. Cab: near-correct answer. Hospital: said the probabilities are about equal (wrong). CRT: 3 of 3 intuitive errors. Adversarial edits: with a 15% blue / 85% green cab setup, asked about a black cab it answered '20%'; reordering Wason cards changed its choice; a CRT item with the wrong 'bat costs $1.00 more than the bat' wording still got $0.10.
limits: One model, one prompt per vignette, many famous items likely in training data. Authors state GPT-3 could not pass as human on these tasks.
agent_relevance: Surface-matching to a famous item is a risk: the model may answer the known version, not the stated version. S1 restating the problem in new surface form helps detect this.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in language models and disappeared in GPT-4
finding: On CRT items and semantic illusions, older models gave intuitive wrong answers at a high rate, GPT-3 text-davinci models most of all. ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly gave correct answers. Prompting for chain of thought, multiple choice or few-shot with correct examples raised GPT-3 accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3 davinci models: on average 84.5% intuitive responses; 86.7% intuitive, 5.3% correct, 8% atypical on 150 CRT tasks. Semantic illusions: 72% intuitive, 26% correct. Correct in text-davinci-003: 10.5% of 200 tasks; ChatGPT 79.5%; GPT-4 97% (Z = -13.87 and -17.35, p < .001). GPT-4 CRT about 98.6% correct, 8% intuitive on semantic illusions. Small base models (e.g. curie, OPT-6.7B) about 13.5% correct, mostly atypical text. Chain-of-thought and few-shot with correct examples raised GPT-3 correct rates (semantic illusions up to 58% correct).
limits: Items are widely published and may be in training data. Tested open-ended answers coded by hand. Models are from 2022 to 2023.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained and larger models mostly stop making CRT-style slips, so the main S1 risk shifts from classic puzzle errors to context cues (planted numbers, authority, framing). Scaffold tests should use fresh, unpublished items.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee and Nguyen (2023/2024) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 and MTurk humans both showed anchoring on a self-chosen random number, conjunction fallacy on a new Linda-like item, and availability pull from an anecdote. Direct Linda was 'patched' by the vendor within a day of a public post.
numbers: Anchoring (N = 30 per condition, t(58)): ChatGPT low anchor mean 20.83, high anchor 105.97, t = 8.78, p < .0001; humans 22.5 and 80.50. Conjunction (artist vs artist who likes to read): ChatGPT chose conjunction 18 of 20; humans 10 of 20 (10 chose the single event). ChatGPT-4 anchoring: 22.0 vs 94.33 (5 trials per cell).
quote: The very next day, perhaps due to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, ChatGPT corrected itself.
limits: Tiny trials for ChatGPT-4. Human sample of 40 on MTurk with low pay. New items are structurally similar, not identical, to Linda. Vendor updates change results over time.
agent_relevance: Even a random number the model itself is asked to produce anchors later estimates in a human-sized way. Do not let the model emit a throwaway guess before it estimates; and re-test model versions, since fixes to famous items are patches, not general repair.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases
finding: Codex and CodeGen are pulled toward an erroneous example function placed in the prompt (anchoring), and their accuracy drops when it is present.
numbers: Print-var anchor functions lowered functional accuracy for all tested numbers of canonical lines. Codex produced 'for var in' in 32% to 61% of solutions and 'print(var)' in 26% to 44% when at least one canonical line was included. Anchor elements also appeared inside correct solutions (3% to 11% for the loop, 1% to 9% for print). Framing prompt: model copied frequent-example pattern in 81% (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) vs 4.5% and 0.0% baseline.
limits: Code generation, HumanEval, 2022 models. The 81% vs 4.5% figure is for a different failure (copying a common pattern), reported in the paper's framing section.
agent_relevance: A wrong earlier attempt or hint placed in context acts as an anchor and lowers accuracy. Supports passing revision only the failing output, not the earlier wrong solution, and keeping a fresh-context path.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: An experimental study
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 shift numeric estimates toward hint values. Stronger models are more consistently anchored. Expert-labelled hints are followed almost always. Chain of thought, 'principles', 'ignore the hint' and reflection prompts did not remove the anchoring; showing both a low and a high hint helped when they bracketed the truth.
numbers: Anchoring index of GPT-4 about 0.45 vs 0.61 for humans in the cited human study. 12 of 12 questions with expert (PTF) hints showed significant anchoring in all models. 11 exceptions out of the question-model grid, 9 from GPT-3.5; time-period questions made up 17% (7 of 42) of questions but 54% (6 of 11) of exceptions. Both-anchor prompt brought GPT-4 close to the benchmark on 8 questions where the two hints fell either side of the truth.
limits: Table output garbled in extraction; statistics reported as t-tests over repeated samples, not preregistered. Authors are high-school students at a school-affiliated lab. Human comparison is to a different study with different method.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for our S1 question: 'ignore it' and CoT do not clear a planted hint in these models. The workable fix is structural: give two opposing hints, or withhold the hint until after the first independent attempt.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld and Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: Instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief bias compared with the matching pretrained model.
numbers: Bias score (treatment minus control rate of choosing the target, range -1 to 1). Belief Invalid: base davinci 0.00, text-davinci-002 0.55, text-davinci-003 0.65. Belief Valid: 0.00, 0.19, 0.21. Mistral-Instruct and Flan-T5 also higher than Mistral and T5 on most scores. GPT-4 used as a reference only.
limits: Biases tested are decoy, certainty and belief bias, not the core anchoring/availability/representativeness set. Pretrained models scored by answer likelihood and instruction-tuned by generation, so the comparison has a method difference. Table in text extraction is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Post-training pushes models toward human-like preference errors. Our agent runs on an instruction-tuned model, so S1 should assume these context-driven pulls are present by default.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (Findings of EMNLP)
finding: Across 13,465 prompts, models show anchoring-like sequential inconsistency, framing bias, group attribution bias and a primacy pull toward early options. Awareness prompts and zero-shot debiasing help a little; few-shot debiasing and counterfactual prompts often make the model fail the task; the 'self-help' method (model rewrites its own prompt to remove biased parts) works best for high-capacity models.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the 'reject' framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. In self-help for anchoring, Llama models changed 40% to 52% of their decisions, indicating inconsistency. Self-help left 0% (Llama-2 13B) and 1.4% (Llama-2 7B) of biased prompts for framing; GPT-4 reduced group attribution elements to 0% and framing to 2.7%.
limits: Admissions task, one high-stakes scenario family. Metrics differ by bias. Few-shot failure partly due to the model collapsing to always admit or always reject.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level debiasing is unreliable and can break instruction following. Weak models cannot debias themselves. Another reason for G5: let code strip or reorder cues, not the model.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, Claude 2, Llama 2 7b/13b/70b) are irrational on classic tasks (Wason, AIDS, hospital, Monty Hall, Linda, birth order), but mostly NOT in the human way. Wrong answers are often non-human-like, and the same prompt gives inconsistent answers across runs.
numbers: GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning in 69.2% of cases; Claude 2 55.0%. Llama 2 7b wrong in 77.5%. Human-like bias with an incorrect answer: GPT-3.5 only 21.7% (50.8% including human-like correct answers). GPT-4 gave human-like responses (correct or not) in 73.3%; Llama 2 13b only 8.3%. Facilitated (easier) versions were not answered better, except the AIDS task. Only Bard identified the Linda problem by name.
limits: Chatbot interfaces for most models (no control of sampling); default settings; small set of tasks (about 12 versions). Pre-2024 models.
agent_relevance: Model errors are partly noise, not just inherited human bias. That supports counting and consistency checks (agreement across fresh samples) over trusting a single answer, while remembering G4: agreement from one model is only a hint.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The bias is in the details: An assessment of cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Large-scale test of 45 LLMs on eight biases with 2.8 million responses. Bias-consistent behavior in 17.8% to 57.3% of instances. Size over 32B reduces bias in 39.5% of cases. Richer prompt detail reduces most biases by up to 14.9% but worsens overattribution by up to 8.8%. Representativeness is the hardest to override.
numbers: Average bias resistance (higher is better): QwQ-32B 0.800 best in table, DeepSeek-R1-Q-32B 0.780, Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.427. Anchoring resistance 0.49 to 0.79 (phi-4 0.680, QwQ-32B 0.776, gemini-1.5-flash 0.787). Representativeness resistance 0.36 to 0.60, lowest of the family (e.g. Qwen2.5-72B 0.405, QwQ-32B 0.587). Framing varies widely (Qwen2.5-1.5B 0.132 to DeepSeek-R1-Q-32B 0.865).
limits: Multiple-choice forced format; scenarios hand-written with psychologists but templated; resistance score is a design-specific measure. Not human-calibrated.
agent_relevance: Size and reasoning training help most on framing and availability, least on representativeness. Our S1 should concentrate on representativeness-type errors (judging by resemblance instead of base rates) even on a strong model.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in large language models
finding: Biases in the judgment family (base rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo) were the hardest to mitigate: prompt-level debiasing backfired for them while it fixed response-style biases. Biases are linearly separable in activations, and steering reduces them but can cost capability.
numbers: Judgment bias shift in points: GPT-4o-mini -4.3, Llama-3.3-70B -7.7, Qwen2.5-72B -2.7 (temperature 0). Prompt debiasing effect: Judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires), Info Processing -1.1%, Social +5.9%, Response position independence +40.5%. Steering cost up to -19.0 points on judgment tasks for Qwen; negligible for Llama. Steering effects correlated across architectures r(246) = .621, p < .001.
quote: prompt-level debiasing substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases
limits: Three models, preprint under review (April 2026). Bias defined against computable ground truth, so some items may differ from human-bias definitions.
agent_relevance: Strong warning for S1: a generic 'avoid anchoring' instruction can hurt exactly the heuristics-and-biases class. Keep debiasing to input restructuring that code controls, and test each at equal tokens (G7).

source: Sumita, Takeuchi and Kashima (2024) Cognitive biases in large language models: A survey and mitigation experiments
finding: Two crowdsourcing debiasing prompts were tried on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 across six biases. 'Awareness reminder' (AwaRe) reduced bias; 'social projection' (answer as others would) had little effect, unlike in humans.
numbers: Six biases tested before and after each prompt; GPT-4 less susceptible to all six than GPT-3.5. Exact per-bias effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Per-bias numbers were not captured in my read of the text, only the direction. Small prompt set. Contradicts CogBias on whether awareness prompts help, which may be due to which biases are tested.
agent_relevance: Mixed evidence for reminder-style prompts. Treat as an arm to test, not a default.

source: Owusu, Wiegreffe and Feldman (2026) Localizing anchoring pathways in language models
finding: In multiple-choice numeric questions from the Open Anchoring Quest dataset, a low or high irrelevant anchor shifts the expected answer in the anchor direction in all four Llama and Qwen models tested, strongest in instruction-tuned Qwen. Anchor circuits transfer within a model but not reliably between base and instruction-tuned versions.
numbers: 100 numeric questions, 20 random option orders per question. Qwen instruct expected-value shift about -0.141 (low) and +0.202 (high); Llama instruct -0.063 and +0.023 (units as in the paper's Table 1, relative to a token-matched control). Attribution metric correlates with the behavioral shift.
limits: Small open models only; multiple-choice format; units of the shift are not clear from my extraction.
agent_relevance: Anchoring in LLMs sits in separate internal pathways that post-training rewires. A fix that works on one model version may not carry to the next.

source: Saeedi, Goodarzi and Canbaz (2025) Heuristics and biases in AI decision-making: Implications for responsible AGI
finding: 1,500 experiments across nine biases on GPT-4o, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1. GPT-4o was strongest overall; Llama 3.1 leaned on heuristics and was inconsistent.
numbers: Gemma 2 reached 63% accuracy on probability-neglect scenarios and 82% on sunk-cost. Models gave opposite framings of identical scenarios in 57%, 74% and 85% of cases for the three models as the text states. One model refused to respond in 33% of experiments.
limits: Small, template-based, abstract-level reading of the numbers; model-to-percentage mapping is from a garbled two-column extraction.
agent_relevance: Consistent with b17: unstable answers across equivalent framings. A consistency check on a reworded copy of the problem is cheap and code-checkable.

source: Araya (2025) Do chains-of-thought of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: Reasoning LLMs given a Bayesian problem do not spontaneously use natural frequencies, whole objects or embodied heuristics, which help humans. When asked to, they use them inconsistently and sometimes still reach wrong answers.
numbers: Qualitative case comparison across several chatbots; example of a final answer of 50% when the right value differed; one chain 'used natural frequencies to change the language in 90%' but kept percentages elsewhere. No aggregate rates.
limits: Few problems, no statistics. Education-focused paper.
agent_relevance: The frequency-format fix (b02) is not applied by the model on its own and is applied unreliably on request. If we want it, code must do the re-expression, not an instruction.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs, heterogeneity and moderators
finding: Anchoring, allowed/forbidden wording and implicit-explicit attitude links had the largest cross-sample heterogeneity, yet no setting variable (US vs elsewhere, lab vs online, order in session) changed any effect much.
numbers: 10 of 32 moderation tests significant, 7 of them among anchoring and allowed/forbidden; none had partial eta squared above .022. Heterogeneity statistics for anchoring: Chicago Q = 312.75, Everest 152.34, babies 59.71, NYC 88.16 (df 35).
quote: Surprisingly, these factors did not produce highly heterogeneous effect sizes.
limits: Moderators tested were few and coarse. Mostly university samples.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is robust across settings. It is not a fragile lab effect, so we should expect a model trained on human text to carry it.

source: Hertwig and Gigerenzer (1999), argument against the heuristics-and-biases reading of Linda
finding: Competing explanation: Gricean relevance. Participants treat the description as informative and the options as meaningful, so the conjunction answer is a sensible inference. The authors report that probability was read as non-mathematical in most paraphrases.
numbers: Paraphrase study: 7 of 39 (18%) responses were mathematical. For similar wording only 7 of 32 (22%) of nonmathematical responses could be read as mathematical. Meaning 'possibility' given 11 times among 56 of 64 (88%) nonmathematical readings.
limits: Self-reported interpretations of a word, small N; does not explain why frequency formats do not always help (Jones et al. 85% vs 81%).
agent_relevance: For an LLM the same pragmatic pull applies: it reads the prompt as relevant. Planted guesses and irrelevant numbers are read as informative, so label them as non-evidence in S1.

source: Toplak et al. (2011), regression results
finding: In hierarchical regressions, after entering intelligence, executive function and thinking dispositions, adding the CRT still explained extra variance on heuristics-and-biases composites.
numbers: Extra variance from CRT in the blocks shown: delta R squared about .025, .080 and .064 in three outcomes (multiple R of the full models .602, .531, .468).
limits: The three outcomes are sub-composites whose labels were garbled in my read; delta R squared values are as printed in the table in order.
agent_relevance: Tendency to stop at the first answer is a separate trait from ability. For the agent that corresponds to 'whether it checks', which the program, not the model, should decide.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022), framing and availability probes
finding: Using framing and availability heuristics as inspiration, the authors found Codex mixes up operation order when a similar frequent pattern exists, and changes output predictably with framing of the same request.
numbers: Availability probe shown in Figure 5; framing probe copy rates 81% (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) vs 4.5% and 0.0% without the framing, as stated in the text of Section 3.3.1.
limits: I read the text summary and not the full appendix tables. Code domain.
agent_relevance: Frequent patterns in training act like availability. Novel-variant tests (changed constants or rules) are a cheap way to detect pattern-copy errors.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023), robustness of intuitive responding in GPT-3
finding: Intuitive errors in GPT-3 could be reduced by prompt changes: multiple-choice format, chain of thought, and few-shot examples with correct (not intuitive) answers.
numbers: Multiple-choice raised correct rates a little: CRT type 1 33.7% correct (Z = -4.5, p < .001), semantic illusions 40% correct. Baseline CRT 11.7% correct vs 72.7% intuitive; semantic illusions 40% correct and 58.3% intuitive under one variant. Chain of thought lifted semantic illusions to 58% correct. Few-shot with intuitive examples kept intuitive responses at 70.7%.
limits: Only text-davinci-003; some conditions mix item types. Numbers are as printed in running text.
agent_relevance: Showing worked examples with the correct, non-intuitive answer helps; showing intuitive examples hurts. Few-shot examples in the scaffold should be checked for being right and non-intuitive.
